CHIEF COMPLAINT
Positive hepatitis C antibody

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a previously healthy individual who presents with positive hepatitis C antibody discovered on routine screening during recent physical examination. Patient reports feeling well and is asymptomatic. He denies any prior knowledge of hepatitis C diagnosis and was surprised by this finding. On further questioning, patient endorses remote history of intravenous drug use but reports being clean for over 15 years.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for jaundice, abdominal pain, fatigue, or other symptoms of liver disease.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant medical conditions. Recent physical examination otherwise unremarkable.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications.

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Hypertension
Diabetes
Depression

SOCIAL HISTORY
History of intravenous drug use in remote past (>15 years ago); patient reports sustained sobriety. Alcohol: occasional beer consumption daily, less than previously. Tobacco: 1-2 cigarettes per day; reports significant reduction from prior use. Married with children.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: All within normal limits
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress, no jaundice noted
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur appreciated
Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi
Abdomen: Bowel sounds present; soft, non-tender; no hepatosplenomegaly
Musculoskeletal/Neurological: No gait disturbance; no peripheral edema

RESULTS
HCV antibody: Positive
AST: 39 U/L (elevated)
ALT: Within normal limits
Albumin: Within normal limits
Total bilirubin: Within normal limits

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hepatitis C infection, newly diagnosed based on positive HCV antibody and mildly elevated AST with otherwise preserved liver function. Plan: (1) Confirmatory testing with HCV RNA and HCV genotype; (2) Assessment of liver fibrosis severity via ultrasound elastography; (3) Family screening with HCV antibody testing for wife and children, with assistance coordinating appointments through family physician; (4) Smoking cessation counseling and consideration for pharmacotherapy in coordination with primary care physician; (5) Follow-up appointment in 3 weeks to review additional test results and determine treatment plan.
